articles.title: OpenShift 4.22: what platform teams should plan for
articles.summary: Red Hat OpenShift 4.22 moves to Kubernetes 1.35, makes cross-cluster VM live migration generally available and refreshes GitOps, Service Mesh and Pipelines. Here is what changes for teams running production clusters in the Gulf.
articles.body:
## What is in the release

OpenShift Container Platform 4.22 is based on Kubernetes 1.35 and CRI-O 1.35. The changes that matter most for teams running production clusters:

- **JobSet controller (generally available).** Run a group of related jobs, such as a distributed training or batch run, as one unit with one status.
- **Lazy image pulling in CRI-O.** Containers can start before a large image has finished downloading, which helps AI and data images that run to many gigabytes.
- **Dynamic Resource Allocation for partitionable devices (Technology Preview).** Hand out slices of an accelerator instead of a whole device.
- **OpenShift Virtualization.** Cross-cluster live migration of virtual machines is now generally available, alongside single-stack IPv6 and MIG vGPU attachment.
- **OpenShift GitOps 1.21.** Ships Argo CD 3.4; the Argo CD CLI and image updater are now generally available.
- **OpenShift Service Mesh 3.4.** Based on Istio 1.30, with FIPS 140-3 support for both sidecar and ambient modes.
- **OpenShift Pipelines 1.22 and Serverless 1.38.** Fleet-wide PipelineRuns and serverless functions as MCP servers arrive as previews.

## Three things to check before you upgrade

1. **Console plug-ins and operators.** Dynamic console plug-ins must move to newer core libraries, and PatternFly 5 is no longer supported. Rebuild and test custom plug-ins on a non-production cluster first, and confirm every operator you run supports 4.22.
2. **Your upgrade path.** OpenShift moves one minor version at a time unless you use the EUS-to-EUS path between Extended Update Support releases. Open the life cycle page, confirm the support dates for your current release and write the path down before you book a window.
3. **How you will use the VM features.** Cross-cluster live migration is useful for data center moves and site maintenance. Try it with non-critical virtual machines and confirm storage and network compatibility between the two clusters.

## What it means for teams in the Gulf

- **Maintenance without leaving the Kingdom.** Moving running virtual machines between two in-country clusters lets you patch or rebuild a site while data stays where your regulator expects it.
- **Better use of expensive accelerators.** Lazy pulling and device partitioning help large AI images start faster and let several workloads share a GPU.
- **Easier compliance conversations.** FIPS 140-3 support in Service Mesh helps when a regulator or customer asks for validated cryptography between services.

## How Elifai helps

We rehearse the upgrade on a copy of your cluster configuration, check every operator and plug-in, and run the production upgrade in an agreed window with a written rollback plan. Our operations center watches the cluster for the following days.

articles.title: RHEL 10.2: post-quantum SSH, kernel livepatching and a better image mode
articles.summary: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2 and 9.8 arrived in May 2026 with post-quantum key exchange for SSH, reboot-free kernel fixes and practical improvements to image mode. Here is what matters for administrators.
articles.body:
## The release at a glance

RHEL 10.2 and RHEL 9.8 were released together in May 2026. RHEL 10.2 is built on the Linux 6.12 long-term support kernel. Three areas deserve attention from operations teams: cryptography, patching and image mode.

## Post-quantum SSH

OpenSSH in RHEL 10.2 supports ML-KEM post-quantum key exchange combined with elliptic curves, including in FIPS mode, and libssh adds hybrid ML-KEM and ECDH methods. The FUTURE system-wide crypto policy now allows only hybrid ML-KEM key exchange.

Before switching policies across a fleet, test with the clients that connect to your servers: older SSH clients, network devices, backup agents and automation tools. Start with a small group:

```bash
sudo update-crypto-policies --show
sudo update-crypto-policies --set FUTURE
# reconnect from every client type you support, then decide
```

## Kernel livepatching

Selected kernel fixes can now be applied without rebooting supported systems. For servers that are hard to restart, such as databases and telecom or payment systems, this narrows the gap between a security advisory and a protected server. Keep scheduled reboots in the plan for cumulative updates.

## Image mode improvements

Image mode manages the operating system as a bootable container image. In 10.2:

- A `--download-only` switch pre-downloads operating system updates, so the maintenance window is spent applying, not downloading.
- Sealed images, in Technology Preview, add cryptographic integrity protection to the image.
- `bcvk`, the bootable containers and virtualization kit, starts short-lived test VMs from an image so you can check a build before rolling it out.

## For developers on the same servers

RHEL 10.2 brings Python 3.14, Go 1.26, OpenJDK 25, Rust 1.92, LLVM 21, PostgreSQL 18, MariaDB 11.8 and PHP 8.4. The Red Hat build of Podman Desktop is available, and an optional AI assistant called goose is offered in the Extensions repository, while the supported RHEL command-line assistant stays in AppStream.

## A rollout plan we use with clients

1. **Pilot** RHEL 10.2 on non-production servers and record what breaks.
2. **Test cryptography** with the FUTURE policy on a few hosts and every client type.
3. **Turn on livepatching** for the servers that are hardest to reboot.
4. **Use image mode** for new, repeatable builds such as edge or appliance-style servers.
5. **Roll out in waves** with Ansible and a written rollback for each wave.

articles.title: A practical guide to private LLMs for IT operations
articles.summary: How to go from a laptop experiment to a governed, in-region model service for your operations team: Ollama to try ideas, vLLM to serve, retrieval over your runbooks, and Kubernetes when you need to scale.
articles.body:
## Start with the job, not the model

Pick one task your engineers repeat every week, such as summarizing an incident, drafting a post-incident review or answering questions from runbooks. Write down how you will measure it before you choose a model: minutes to triage, how much an engineer has to edit, or how often the answer cites the right runbook.

## Step 1: try ideas on a laptop with Ollama

Ollama runs open models locally with one command. It is the fastest way to test prompts on sample, non-sensitive data.

```bash
ollama run llama3.2
```

Keep a small set of real questions and the answers you expect. You will reuse it at every step.

## Step 2: serve a model with vLLM

When more than one person needs the model, serve it. vLLM is an open-source inference engine with an OpenAI-compatible API, so most tools can talk to it without changes.

```bash
pip install vllm
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct --port 8000
```

```bash
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this alert: disk 92% on db-01"}]}'
```

Run it on a GPU server in your own data center or in a cloud region inside the country, so prompts and logs never leave it.

## Step 3: ground answers in your runbooks

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) searches your own documents and hands the relevant passages to the model with the question. For operations this means answers that quote your runbook, not the internet. Index runbooks, past incident reviews and architecture notes, and ask the model to cite which document it used.

## Step 4: scale and govern on Kubernetes

For many teams and models, move serving onto your platform. Red Hat AI 3, released in October 2025, brought distributed inference built on the open-source llm-d project and vLLM to Red Hat OpenShift AI. At Red Hat Summit in May 2026, Red Hat announced Red Hat AI 3.4 with governed model access, agent operations and built-in safety controls. llm-d itself is an open project you can study on GitHub.

## Guardrails that matter in operations

- **Suggest, do not act.** The model proposes; an engineer approves any change to production.
- **Log everything.** Keep every prompt, retrieved document and answer for audit.
- **Keep data in region.** Serve models where your data is allowed to be.
- **Measure against a baseline.** Run in shadow mode next to your normal process, and stop if it does not help.

## A six-week plan

1. **Weeks 1–2:** choose one use case, collect 50 real examples and agree how to score them.
2. **Weeks 3–4:** serve a model with vLLM, add retrieval over runbooks and run in shadow mode.
3. **Weeks 5–6:** compare against the baseline and decide whether to scale, change the model or stop.

Our learning hub has a free course that follows these steps with videos and GitHub projects.

articles.title: Choosing a cloud region in Saudi Arabia in 2026
articles.summary: Two years ago a Saudi organization that needed in-Kingdom hosting had a short list. By the end of 2026 almost every major provider will run a region inside the country. More choice is good news, but it also makes the decision harder. This guide sets out what is available, what the regulations actually ask for, and how we help clients choose.
articles.body:
## Who runs a region in the Kingdom
ProviderSaudi locationStatus, November 2026
Google CloudDammamGenerally available
Oracle Cloud InfrastructureJeddah, RiyadhGenerally available
Alibaba CloudRiyadh, operated with Saudi Cloud Computing CompanyGenerally available
Amazon Web ServicesSaudi Arabia regionAnnounced for launch by December 2026
Microsoft AzureSaudi Arabia regionAnnounced for the fourth quarter of 2026
Availability changes quickly, and not every service launches in every region on day one. Before committing, check the provider's own region page for the specific services you need, such as managed Kubernetes, GPU instances or a particular database engine. ## What the rules actually require Three sets of requirements usually shape the decision: - **The Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL)**, enforceable since September 2024 and overseen by SDAIA, governs how personal data is processed and when it may be transferred outside the Kingdom. - **The National Cybersecurity Authority's controls**, in particular the Essential Cybersecurity Controls (ECC-2:2024) and the Cloud Cybersecurity Controls (CCC-2:2024), set expectations for how systems are secured, including those run by cloud providers and managed-service partners. - **Sector rules** from regulators such as SAMA for financial services, which can be stricter than the national baseline. In practice, most of our Saudi clients choose to keep production data and its backups in-Kingdom by default, and document any exception. That removes a whole class of questions from every audit. ## Four questions that decide the region 1. **Where must the data live?** If the answer is "in the Kingdom, including backups and logs", rule out any design that ships telemetry or snapshots to another region by default. 2. **Which services do you actually need?** A region that lacks your database engine or GPU type forces workarounds that cost more than a slightly higher unit price elsewhere. 3. **What do you already run?** An existing Oracle estate often lands best on OCI; a team fluent in Kubernetes can move between GKE, EKS and OKE with little friction. 4. **How will you recover?** Check whether the provider offers more than one Saudi region or zone, and plan disaster recovery inside the Kingdom if your rules require it. ## Keeping multi-cloud manageable Many Gulf organizations end up with two clouds and a private VMware or OpenShift estate. That is fine if the operating model is shared. We standardize on infrastructure as code with Terraform, GitOps delivery with Argo CD, one observability stack built on OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Grafana, and one set of runbooks. The result is that an engineer on call does not need to remember which console a workload lives in. ## How Elifai helps We run region-selection workshops for Saudi organizations, build landing zones in the chosen region, map the design to NCA and PDPL requirements, and then operate the platform around the clock with named engineers and written service levels.

articles.title: Mapping NCA cybersecurity controls to Kubernetes
articles.summary: Most Saudi compliance teams know the NCA control documents well. Most platform teams know Kubernetes well. The gap is in between: which cluster setting proves which control, and where the evidence comes from. This guide shows how we close that gap on OpenShift, GKE, EKS and OKE.
articles.body:
## Start from the control domains, not the tools The Essential Cybersecurity Controls (ECC-2:2024) are organized into domains covering governance, defense, resilience, third-party and cloud security, and industrial systems. The Cloud Cybersecurity Controls (CCC-2:2024) add requirements for cloud providers and for organizations that use them. Rather than starting with a list of Kubernetes features, we start with the domains that touch a platform and ask, for each one, what an auditor will ask to see. ## A working map
Control areaWhat we configureEvidence we hand over
Identity and access managementSSO to the cluster through your identity provider, role-based access per namespace, no shared admin accounts, short-lived credentialsRBAC export, access review records, login audit logs
Data protection and cryptographyEncryption at rest with customer-managed keys, TLS everywhere, secrets in Vault or a cloud KMS rather than plain Kubernetes secretsKey policy, certificate inventory, secret-store configuration
Vulnerability and patch managementImage scanning in the pipeline, signed images only, scheduled node and OS patching for RHEL or Ubuntu workersScan reports, admission-policy logs, patch compliance dashboard
Event logging and monitoringAPI server audit logging, central log retention in-Kingdom, alerting into a staffed operations centerRetention settings, sample alerts, incident tickets
Configuration and change managementAll cluster state in Git, changes through pull requests, policy-as-code (OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno) blocking unsafe workloadsGit history, approval records, policy reports
Resilience and backupMulti-zone control plane, Velero or native backups stored in-Kingdom, restore tests on a scheduleBackup job history, signed restore-test results
Third-party and cloud securityDocumented shared-responsibility split with the cloud provider and with us as managed-service partnerResponsibility matrix, provider attestations
Exact control numbers differ between document versions and between ECC and CCC, so we keep the mapping in a spreadsheet tied to the version your regulator expects, and update it when NCA publishes a revision. ## Make the evidence automatic The expensive part of compliance is collecting evidence by hand before every audit. We avoid that by producing evidence as a side effect of running the platform: policy reports from the admission controller, patch status from the fleet dashboard, backup and restore results from scheduled jobs, and access reviews from the identity provider. A quarterly export then becomes a pack your compliance team can submit as it is. ## Common gaps we find - Cluster-admin rights shared by a whole team, with no record of who did what. - Audit logs enabled but shipped to a region outside the Kingdom by default. - Backups that exist but have never been restored. - Kubernetes secrets stored in Git with base64 encoding mistaken for encryption. ## How Elifai helps We run a two-week gap assessment against the control versions you are measured on, fix what we find, and then operate the platform with the evidence pipeline in place, so every quarter's audit pack is ready before anyone asks for it. This article is general guidance, not legal advice. Always confirm requirements with your compliance function and the current NCA publications.

articles.title: AIOps for Gulf enterprises: where to start
articles.summary: Every operations team in the Gulf is being asked what it is doing with AI. The honest answer for most is "not much yet", and that is a reasonable place to start. AIOps works best when it begins small, with a clear before-and-after measure, and with people in charge of every change to production.
articles.body:
## Two use cases that pay back first

### 1. Alert correlation

A single failing database can trigger hundreds of alerts across the services that depend on it. Correlation groups them into one incident with a likely cause, so the on-call engineer starts from the problem rather than from the noise. This is usually the fastest win because the data already exists in your monitoring tools.

### 2. Incident summaries and ticket triage

Large language models are good at reading timelines, logs and chat threads and turning them into a clear summary. Used for incident reviews and for routing tickets to the right team, they save hours each week without making any change to production systems.

## A safe six-week pilot

1. **Weeks 1 and 2, baseline.** Measure what happens today: alerts per incident, time to acknowledge, time to restore, and hours spent writing incident reviews.
2. **Weeks 3 and 4, shadow mode.** Run the AI alongside your team on real incidents. It suggests, people decide, and every suggestion is scored.
3. **Weeks 5 and 6, decide.** Compare against the baseline. Keep what clearly helped, drop what did not, and agree which actions may ever be automated.

## What to measure

- Alerts per incident, before and after correlation.
- Mean time to acknowledge and mean time to restore.
- Share of AI suggestions engineers accepted.
- Cost per incident handled, including model usage.

## Guardrails for regulated environments

For Saudi and Gulf organizations subject to PDPL, NCA controls or sector rules, keep three guardrails from day one: run models where your data is allowed to be, which may mean a private model in-Kingdom; log every prompt and response used in an incident; and require a named engineer to approve any action that changes production.

## How Elifai helps

We run AIOps readiness assessments, build the correlation and summary pipelines on top of the telemetry you already have, and operate them alongside our 24/7 managed service, so the AI and the people who act on it are the same team.
